overview.body:
**Ebisu** ​(*ebisu*) — ‌Fishermen, ‌Commerce, ​Luck — ​belongs ​to ​the Japanese ​tradition. ‌The ​name means ​"The ‌foreigner, ​straggler"[^1].

Ebisu ‌is ​the ‌cheerful god ​of ​fishermen, ​commerce, and ​honest ​labour, ‌the most ​approachable ‌of ​the Seven ‌Gods ​of ‌Fortune.

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the ​name as ​**Ebisu**. ‌The ‌plain ASCII ‌form ​*ebisu* ​is the ‌modern ​Hepburn ​romanization; the ‌restoration ​capitalizes ​the conventional ‌spelling. ​Because the ‌Japanese ​source ​script uses ​logographic ​characters ‌whose distinctive ‌visual ​form ‌cannot be ​conveyed ​in ‌the basic ‌Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and because ​no ‌diacritic ​or special ​letter ​is ‌added in ​this ​restoration, ​the name ‌is ​placed ​in Tier ​2. ‌The ​Unicode form ‌remains ​the ‌philologically complete ​reference, ‌while ‌the ASCII ​spelling ​is ​a practical ​convenience ‌for ‌the domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Japanese ‌characters as ​**恵比寿**. Etymologically ​it means ​"The foreigner, ​straggler"[^1].

The ​name Ebisu ‌is connected ​with the ​Old Japanese ‌word *ebisu* ​or *emishi*, ‌meaning "stranger," ​"barbarian," or ‌"one who ​drifts ashore." ​Mythologically he is ​the malformed ​son of ​Izanagi and ‌Izanami, cast ​away into ‌the sea ​because he ‌could not ​stand at ‌the age ​of three. ‌He became ​the patron ​of fishermen ‌and, later, ‌of commerce ‌and daily livelihood.

​The ASCII ​form *ebisu* ‌survives only ​because the ​early domain-name ‌system could ​not carry ​Japanese characters ‌or diacritics; ​it is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ​an ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Ebisu** gives ‌the conventional ​Hepburn romanization with ‌initial capitalization, ​the standard ​scholarly way ‌to cite ‌a proper ‌name in ‌romanized Japanese. ​The name ‌is Tier ​2 because ​the restoration ​does not ‌add a ​distinctive diacritic ​or special ​letter absent ‌from the ASCII ​form.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**e** → ​**E** — ‌Same, capitalized
​- **b** ‌→ **b** ​— Same
‌- **i** ‌→ **i** ​— Same
​- **s** ​→ **s** ​— Same
‌- **u** ‌→ **u** ​— Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/e.bi.sɯ/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'EBISU' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Ebisu ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*ebisu* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Ebisu** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Ebisu** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*ebisu* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Ebisu ​presides over ‌fishing, commerce, ‌and ​honest labour. ​He is ​the ​most approachable ​of the ‌Seven ​Gods of ​Fortune, ‌protector of ​small shopkeepers, ‌sailors, ​and anyone ‌who earns ​a ​living by ​daily effort. ​Unlike ​the more ‌exalted kami ​of ‌heaven, Ebisu ​belongs to ‌the ​world of ‌work ​and the ‌sea.

The ​domain ​of **Ebisu** ‌is understood ‌within ‌the broader ​Japanese religious ​landscape ‌as both ​a specific ​functional ‌sphere and ​a node ​in ‌a network ​of ‌kami, buddhas, ​and local ​spirits. ​Shrines, temples, ​and household ‌rites ‌all invoke ​the figure ‌in ​ways that ​blur strict ‌boundaries ‌between Shinto ‌and Buddhist ‌practice[^3]. ​The restoration ‌**Ebisu** ​therefore names ​not only ​a ‌mythic person ​but a ​living ​field of ‌ritual activity: ​pilgrimage, ​festival, iconography, ​and prayer ‌continue ​to define ‌what the ​name ‌means in ​contemporary ‌Japan. This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" ​context is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
The *Kojiki* ​and *Nihon ‌Shoki* recount ‌that Ebisu ​was born ​from the ​improper union ​of Izanagi ​and Izanami ‌before their ​marriage rites ​had been ‌properly performed. ​Because he could ‌not stand ​at the ‌age of ​three, he ​was placed ​in a ​boat of ​reeds and ‌cast off ​to the ‌sea. He ​drifted to the ‌land of ​*Atsuta* or ‌*Nishinomiya*, where ​he became ‌a tutelary ​deity of ​fishermen. His ‌separation from ‌the heavenly ‌kami and ​his survival ​by the ‌sea make him ​the patron ​of those ‌who live ​on the ​margins.

The ‌narrative of ​**Ebisu** participates ‌in the ​larger mythic ​program of ​the *Kojiki* ​and *Nihon Shoki*: ‌to explain ‌the origins ​of the ‌imperial house, ​the division ​of divine ‌labour, and ‌the relationship ‌between the ‌human and ​kami worlds. ‌Because these ​chronicles were compiled ​in the ​eighth century ‌under imperial ​patronage, the ​myths also ​serve a ‌political theology, ​grounding earthly ​authority in ​divine descent ‌and cosmic ​order[^3]. Read comparatively, ‌the story ​of ebisu ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses genealogy, ‌descent from ​heaven, and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ‌construct a ‌coherent sacred ​history.

sources.citation: Shinto: The Kami Way, Ono Sokyo, 1962.

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in ​​Japanese ​characters ​as ‌**恵比寿** ​— ​Japanese ‌logographic ​and ‌syllabic ​script ‌​(kanji ​plus ​kana ​where ​attested), ‌attested ​in ‌the ​classical ‌Japanese ​‌sources. ​The ‌script ​is ​written ‌top-to-bottom ‌in ‌traditional ​contexts ​and ‌​left-to-right ​in ‌modern ​reproductions[^1].

​The ‌scholarly ​transliteration ‌is ​*Ebisu* ​(Hepburn ​​romanization ‌with ‌initial ​capitalization), ‌giving ​the ​normalized ‌reading ‌//e.bi.sɯ//.

‌The ‌​characters ‌恵比寿 ​are ​*ateji* ​chosen ‌primarily ​for ​their ​auspicious ‌meanings: ​​恵 ​(blessing), ‌比 ​(compare), ‌寿 ​(longevity). ‌The ​older ‌spelling ‌夷 ​​(*ebisu*) ​explicitly ​records ‌the ‌"foreigner" ​etymology.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are the ​earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Ebisu**, ​although the ​figure ‌may have ​circulated in ​oral and ‌local cult ​forms ‌long before ​the eighth ‌century. In ​the ​chronicles, Ebisu ​appears as ​one of ​the ‌Seven Lucky ​Gods, patron ‌of fishermen ​and ‌merchants, of ​obscure origins ‌possibly linked ​to ‌Hiruko, embedded ​in the ​imperial genealogy ‌and the ‌narrative ‌of cosmic ​order[^1]. The ​*Kojiki* account ‌tends ​to privilege ​the mythic ‌lineage leading ​to ​Amaterasu and ‌the imperial ​house, while ‌the ​*Nihon Shoki* ​often presents ​variant traditions ​side ‌by side, ‌preserving conflicting ​genealogies and ‌episodes.

​Because both ​texts were ‌compiled under ‌imperial patronage, ‌their ‌portrayal of ​Ebisu is ‌never purely ​"mythological" ​in a ​neutral sense; ‌it is ​also ​a statement ​about legitimacy, ‌territory, and ​the ​proper ordering ​of the ‌human and ​divine ‌worlds[^2]. Modern ​readers must ‌therefore distinguish ​between the ‌older ‌narrative strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and ​the ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

shinto-sources.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Ebisu** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Ebisu ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Ebisu ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Ebisu** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Ebisu ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Ebisu through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
